name: Prout's Brown
lede: Prout's Brown is a warm, transparent watercolour brown named for the English artist Samuel Prout, sold in the nineteenth century under the name Liquid Prout's Brown.

sections.title: A painter's ink-brown
sections.body:
John Scoffern Salter's 1869 revision of Field's treatise describes, under indelible brown inks, "a beautiful transparent brown for water-colour artists, known as Liquid Prout's Brown" [1]. Salter records that it was seemingly named for the English topographical artist Samuel Prout (1783 to 1852), known for architectural watercolours of continental cities [1]. He suggests it was built on bistre or sepia, two older brown pigments, but used with less binding medium, closer to an ink than a paint [1][2].

Ridgway catalogued it in 1912 on plate XV, hue 15 prime, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists two further names on the same plate: Raw, dated to 1600, and Terra Umber, dated to 1738 [3].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: In LCH terms the swatch measures lightness 40, chroma 23, hue 66 degrees, a warm, medium-dark brown [4]. Its nearest library neighbor is [[beige-brown|Beige Brown]], about 2.5 units away, with [[pale-brown|Pale Brown]] close behind [4]. Next to [[sepia]] or [[bistre]] it reads as the warmer, more orange one [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this brown, as photographed, in 5,091 of 23,781 paintings, about 21 percent, making it one of the most common tones in the set [5]. It covers over 90 percent of the canvas in several Chinese and Japanese ink landscapes, including a 1279 painting of geese in flight and a 1680 landscape by Kano Chikanobu [5]. These counts are computed color matches on aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [5].

origin.first_recorded: mid-19th century, as a watercolour ink; catalogued by Ridgway in 1912
